'''Ascon''' is a family of [[lightweight cipher|lightweight]] [[authenticated cipher]]s and [[Hash function|hash functions]] that have been selected by the U.S. [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST) for cryptography on resource-constrained devices in 2025, specified in NIST SP 800-232.{{sfn|NIST|2023a}}<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2025-08-13 |title=NIST Finalizes 'Lightweight Cryptography' Standard to Protect Small Devices |url=https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/08/nist-finalizes-lightweight-cryptography-standard-protect-small-devices |journal=NIST |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite report |url=https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/232/ipd |title=Ascon-Based Lightweight Cryptography Standards for Constrained Devices: Authenticated Encryption, Hash, and Extendable Output Functions |last1=Sönmez Turan |first1=Meltem |last2=McKay |first2=Kerry |last3=Chang |first3=Donghoon |last4=Kang |first4=Jinkeon |last5=Kelsey |first5=John |date=2024-11-08 |publisher=National Institute of Standards and Technology |issue=NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-232 (Withdrawn) |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
Ascon was developed in 2014 by a team of researchers from [[Graz University of Technology]], [[Infineon Technologies]], Lamarr Security Research, and [[Radboud University]].{{sfn|NIST|2023b}} The cipher family was chosen as a finalist of the [[CAESAR Competition]]{{sfn|NIST|2023b}} in February 2019.

NIST announced its decision on February 7, 2023{{sfn|NIST|2023b}} with the following steps that lead to its standardization:{{sfn|NIST|2023a}}
* Publication of NIST IR 8454<ref>{{Cite web |last=Computer Security Division |first=Information Technology Laboratory |date=2023-06-16 |title=NIST IR 8454: Status Report of Lightweight Cryptography Final Round {{!}} CSRC |url=https://csrc.nist.gov/News/2023/nist-ir-8454-lightweight-crypto-final-report |access-date=2025-08-13 |website=CSRC {{!}} NIST |language=EN-US}}</ref> describing the process of evaluation and selection that was used;
* Preparation of a new draft<ref>{{Cite web |last=Computer Security Division |first=Information Technology Laboratory |date=2024-11-06 |title=NIST Invites Public Comments on SP 800-232 {{!}} CSRC |url=https://csrc.nist.gov/News/2024/nist-invites-public-comments-on-sp-800-232 |access-date=2025-08-13 |website=CSRC {{!}} NIST |language=EN-US}}</ref> for public comments<ref>{{Cite web |title=Compilation of Public Comments on SP 800 |url=https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/232/ipd/docs/sp800-232-ipd-public-comments-received.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250403024753/https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/232/ipd/docs/sp800-232-ipd-public-comments-received.pdf |archive-date=2025-04-03}}</ref>;
* Public workshop held on June 21–22, 2023.[https://csrc.nist.gov/events/2023/lightweight-cryptography-workshop-2023]
NIST finalized the standard on August 13, 2025, releasing it as "Ascon-Based Lightweight Cryptography Standards for Constrained Devices" (NIST Special Publication 800-232).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-13 |title=Ascon-Based Lightweight Cryptography Standards for Constrained Devices: Authenticated Encryption, Hash, and Extendable Output Functions |url=https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/232/final |access-date=2025-08-23 |website=[[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] |doi=10.6028/NIST.SP.800-232}}</ref>

== Design ==
The design is based on a [[sponge construction]] along the lines of SpongeWrap and MonkeyDuplex. This design makes it easy to reuse Ascon in multiple ways (as a cipher, [[cryptographic hash|hash]], or a [[Message authentication code|MAC]]).{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=17}} As of February 2023, the Ascon suite contained seven ciphers,{{sfn|NIST|2023b}} including:{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2021|pp=4-5}}
* Ascon-128 and Ascon-128a authenticated ciphers;
* Ascon-Hash cryptographic hash;
* Ascon-Xof [[extendable-output function]];
* Ascon-80pq cipher with an "increased" 160-bit key.

The main components have been borrowed from other designs:{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=17}}
* substitution layer utilizes a modified [[S-box]] from the {{mvar|χ}} function of [[Keccak]];
* permutation layer functions are similar to the <math>\Sigma</math> of [[SHA-2]].

=== Parameterization ===
The ciphers are parameterizable by the [[key length]] ''k'' (up to 128 bits), "rate" ([[Block size (cryptography)|block size]]) ''r'', and two numbers of [[Round (cryptography)|rounds]] ''a'', ''b''. All algorithms support [[authenticated encryption]] with plaintext P and [[additional authenticated data]] A (that remains unencrypted). The encryption input also includes a public [[Cryptographic nonce|nonce]] N, the output - [[authentication tag]] T, size of the ciphertext C is the same as that of P. The decryption uses N, A, C, and T as inputs and produces either P or signals verification failure if the message has been altered. Nonce and tag have the same size as the key K (''k'' bits).{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=2}}

In the CAESAR submission, two sets of parameters were recommended:{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=2}}
{| class="wikitable"
|+ Suggested parameters, bits
|-
! Name !! ''k'' !! ''r'' !! ''a'' !! ''b''
|-
| Ascon-128 || 128 || 64 || 12 || 6
|-
| Ascon-128a || 128 || 128 || 12 || 8
|}

=== Padding ===
The data in both A and P is padded with a single bit with the value of 1 and a number of zeros to the nearest multiple of {{mvar|r}} bits. As an exception, if A is an empty string, there is no padding at all.{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=4}} 

=== State ===
The state consists of 320 bits, so the capacity <math>c=320-r</math>.{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=3}} The state is initialized by an initialization vector IV (constant for each cipher type, e.g., hex 
80400c0600000000 for Ascon-128) concatenated with K and N.{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|pp=4-5}} 

=== Transformation ===
The initial state is transformed by applying {{mvar|a}} times the transformation function {{mvar|p}}  (<math>p^a</math>). On encryption, each word of A || P is XORed into the state and the {{mvar|p}} is applied {{mvar|b}} times (<math>p^b</math>). The ciphertext C is contained in the first {{mvar|r}} bits of the result of the XOR. Decryption is near-identical to encryption.{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=3}} The final stage that produces the tag T consists of another application of <math>p^a</math>; the special values are XORed into the last {{mvar|c}} bits after the initialization, the end of A, and before the finalization.{{sfn|Dobraunig|Eichlseder|Mendel|Schläffer|2016|p=4}}

Transformation {{mvar|p}} consists of three layers:
* <math>p_C</math>, XORing the [[round constant]]s;
* <math>p_S</math>, application of 5-bit [[S-box]]es;
* <math>p_L</math>, application of [[linear diffusion]].
